teaser: A passkey's PRF bytes compute the top vault, a keyring for every other key, so no key is stored and the passkey is a lock, not an identity.
core_idea: An end-to-end, client-side account with no sign-in to the site: a passkey with the WebAuthn PRF extension for 32 bytes only the user's authenticator can produce for the site, and sgit vaults. Because sgit vault keys are made in the client, the browser computes the top vault's key and id from the PRF bytes with HKDF, so nothing has to be stored or found first; the top is the root of the chain of vaults that hold other vaults' keys, holding the keys of the reading and notes vaults, received read keys, the access key, and key pairs that are generated at random and never derived from the passkey. The user is signed in where they already are, Apple, Google or Microsoft, and the vault travels with that passkey store. Several passkeys give several tops, chosen in the store's own picker, for separating admin from reader; keys move between tops by copying and rotating; a top is retired by deleting its vault, after which its passkey opens nothing. Recovery is the top key saved once. PRF works in Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello and Firefox. The page that holds keys loads no third-party scripts.

nodes.label: Signed in where you already are
nodes.summary: Apple, Google or Microsoft syncs the passkey store; the site is never signed in to, and the vault travels with the store.

nodes.label: Passkey with PRF
nodes.summary: 32 bytes only your authenticator produces for this site, the same on synced devices.

nodes.label: The top vault, computed
nodes.summary: Key and id computed from the PRF bytes with HKDF; the root of the chain, a keyring and nothing else.

nodes.label: What the top holds
nodes.summary: The keys of the vaults below, received read keys, the access key, and the key pairs for the site.

nodes.label: Where the key lives: nowhere
nodes.summary: sgit keys are made in the client, so the top is computed, not stored; delete the vault and the passkey opens nothing.

nodes.label: The top key, saved once
nodes.summary: Shown at first run and kept in a password manager; opens the top without the passkey.

nodes.label: No third-party scripts where keys live
nodes.summary: Storage is per origin; the unlock page loads nothing it did not build.

nodes.label: PRF support in 2026
nodes.summary: Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello, Firefox.

nodes.label: Accounts with no server
nodes.summary: Any static site: sign in, open your own data on any device, unreadable by the operator.

nodes.label: Where the passkey lives
nodes.summary: A synced provider or a hardware key gives every device; a clean browser gives one device plus recovery; Chrome's own store has no PRF.

nodes.label: A lock, not an identity
nodes.summary: Key pairs are generated at random and stored in the top, never derived from the passkey, so the identity survives any change of lock.

nodes.label: Several passkeys, several tops
nodes.summary: Distinct user handles and names, the store's picker as the switch; an admin top on a hardware key, a reader top in the cloud.

nodes.label: Move and retire
nodes.summary: Copy an entry between tops, rotate what moved for security, delete a retired top with the write key, then delete the passkey in the store.

nodes.label: Vaults all the way down
nodes.summary: The pattern already in use: vaults that hold the keys of other vaults, so a read key to one child exposes nothing above it.

quotes.text: The answer, after the research, is that it is not kept anywhere. It is computed.
quotes.why: The answer to where the top key lives.

quotes.text: More important, the passkey is a lock, not an identity: it opens the top and does nothing else.
quotes.why: Why the key pairs are never derived from the passkey.

quotes.text: Deleting either side retires the pair.
quotes.why: The coupling between a passkey and the vault it computes.
